newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa stock plunges ownership limit law.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa stock plunges ownership limit law.

text.p: The stock of Deutsche Lufthansa AG plunged by as much 5 percent Tuesday as the German government stunned international investors with a draft law imposing limits on foreign ownership in the airline.

Lufthansa stock dived 1.25 marks to a low of 20.60 after the Transport Ministry proposed measures to restrict foreign ownership of the airline to 50 percent in preparation for the flotation of the state's remaining 36 percent stake this year.
The restrictions are standard for airlines and are required by international air laws, which demand that flag carriers have domestic ownership.

But dealers said investors had been scared by clauses requiring Lufthansa ordinary shares to be converted to stock with restricted transfer rights and giving Lufthansa the right in some cases to force foreign investors to sell their shares.
"The whole deal is making people less sure of the company," said one trader.

But airline analysts said the panic was overdone. The experience of other privatised flag carriers with similar foreign ownership limits, such as British Airways Plc, showed the risk of compulsory share repurchases was not great.
"People are over-reacting to the risk of forced sales. In 10 years, British Airways has not got close to its limit," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Chris Tarry.
British Airways currently had foreign ownership of around 23 percent, comparable with the estimated 20 percent international shareholding base in Lufthansa, he said.

Lufthansa welcomed the draft law as an "appropriate measure" and said it paved the way for the sale of Bonn's remaining stake, worth about three billion marks ($1.9 billion), around the fourth quarter of this year.

A spokesman said that assuming the law was passed in the coming months, Lufthansa shareholders would be called on to approve the possible implications for its shares at a meeting to be held in late June.

If more than 40 percent of Lufthansa shares fell into foreign hands, it would be allowed to buy back its own stock. If the proportion rose above 45 percent, a new share issue from which existing shareholders would be excluded would be possible.
In the extreme case that foreign shareholders gained more than 50 percent of the airline's shares, it would be permitted to force foreign shareholders to sell their stock.
After their initial plunge, Lufthansa stock pulled back from its lows to trade down 80 pfennigs at 21.05 marks toward the end of bourse dealing.
